# Choosing the right AI courses to build a skills wallet for your career


Learn how to choose the right AI course for your career goals, build practical AI skills and find training that matches your experience level.


Published Nov 23, 2026


ByNate Gulley


Published Nov 23, 2026


## At a glance


-


**Start with clear goals:** Think about what you want AI to help you do, then look for courses that build skills for reaching your goals.


-


**Build a learning foundation:** Start with AI basics, like prompting and responsible use, before diving into specialized topics.


-


**Test your skills:** As you progress, choose courses that earn credentials and build capabilities you can apply to your role.


More than half of American employees now use AI at their jobs, according to a recent[Gallup poll](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/712736/organizational-adoption-jumps-six-points.aspx) . But simply using AI at work may not be enough to stand out. As more employers embrace the technology, it’s important for workers to build what I call an AI skills wallet—capabilities you can apply, demonstrate and grow. Figuring out how to do that can feel daunting. What training should you take? How much do you already need to know about AI? And which course is right for your job?


Verizon’s AI Skills for America offers free AI training for different experience levels and career goals–the types of learning opportunities I help workers connect with. In my role as a solutions consultant, I work with global partners across industries to identify skills their employees need and help develop them. That includes AI readiness. I’ve worked with a wide spectrum of learners, from people nervous about using AI for the first time to those developing capabilities far beyond my own.


Headlines might have you believe that AI is coming for ** your job. While I don’t think that’s true, I do believe it is absolutely coming *to* your job, if it’s not there already. And no matter your skill level, there’s a course out there to prove you’re ready to take it on. Here’s what I tell people who are looking to skill up.


## Think about what you want to do with AI


Before browsing courses, consider first what you’d like to be able to do. Do you want to:


-


Become more effective in your current role?
-


Get ready for your next career move?
-


Have a general understanding of everyday AI use?


Now think about what you’re comfortable doing with AI, what you’d like to try and where you need guidance. If you’re interested in a particular job, look at the skills successful professionals in that field possess. Are there any gaps between their capabilities and yours?


## Connect learning to your goals


When you connect a course to your aspirations, learning feels more meaningful. You’re also more likely to stick with it when the material gets challenging. And I’ve found that the best learning experiences are indeed challenging.


For example, finding ways to make your workday more productive can be motivating. Or perhaps you want to use AI to improve presentations, analyze information or take on new responsibilities at work. Identifying courses that teach the specific skills you want to build can give you a clear target and let you achieve small wins along the way.


When you’re reading a course’s description and learning objectives, think about what skills it will help you develop, how you’ll practice them and how you’ll demonstrate what you’ve learned. Don’t be afraid to experiment, either. If you’re 20 minutes into a course and realize it isn’t teaching what you need, it’s okay to choose something else.


## Build your AI skills with free training from Verizon.


[Learn more](https://www.verizon.com/about/responsibility/human-prosperity/workforce-development/ai-learning?utm_source=pace-story-right-ai-course-for-your-career-nov-26-350oBz&utm_campaign=default&utm_medium=default)


## Establish your learning foundation


I think about learning as a pyramid. Before moving into specialized tools and applications, you need a strong base. With AI, that starts with understanding what it can do, communicating effectively with AI tools and recognizing when they’re appropriate—or not—for a task or project.


If you don’t have a good grasp of what AI is or how it works, a broad introductory course may be the right starting point. Courses like[Google AI Essentials Specialization](https://www.verizon.com/ai-skills/courses/google-ai-essentials-specialization?utm_source=pace-story-right-ai-course-for-your-career-nov-26-350oBz&utm_campaign=default&utm_medium=default) can help you understand the technology and its potential applications. A good example of a fundamental AI skill is prompting, or the[commands you give AI to create something](https://www.verizon.com/ai-skills/courses/getting-started-with-generative-ai?utm_source=pace-story-right-ai-course-for-your-career-nov-26-350oBz&utm_campaign=default&utm_medium=default) . Understanding how to provide thoughtful instructions and relevant context can significantly improve AI-generated responses.


But technical skills are only part of the foundation.[Responsible AI use](https://www.verizon.com/ai-skills/courses/use-ai-responsibly?utm_source=pace-story-right-ai-course-for-your-career-nov-26-350oBz&utm_campaign=default&utm_medium=default) matters, too. You need to know which tools your organization approves, how to protect sensitive information and when to question an AI-generated result. Just because AI can complete a task doesn’t mean it should. I’ve seen people spend more time trying to get AI to do something than it would have taken to do the work without AI.


That brings me to one skill that can’t be underestimated in the age of AI: critical thinking. AI can generate ideas, synthesize information and solve problems. But we still need human judgment to evaluate its outputs, recognize limitations and make decisions. In 2025, for example, Coursera saw a 185% increase in enrollments in critical-thinking courses. To me, that’s a sign that people and organizations recognize the importance of keeping human capabilities sharp as AI becomes more prevalent.


## Expand AI skills you’ve learned


Once you’re comfortable with the fundamentals, your next course should stretch your capabilities. Think about a problem you need to solve. Is there a recurring workflow that AI could improve? Is your team struggling to make sense of large amounts of information?


Get clear on your problem first, then find learning opportunities that address it. For example, imagine you work in customer service. Your team collects valuable information about customer experiences, but there’s too much data to review efficiently. Learning to use[AI for data analysis](https://www.verizon.com/ai-skills/courses/ai-for-data-analysis?utm_source=pace-story-right-ai-course-for-your-career-nov-26-350oBz&utm_campaign=default&utm_medium=default) could help you identify pain points, uncover trends and recommend improvements.


For more advanced learners, AI agents are another area worth exploring. Rather than using an AI chatbot for individual requests, you might learn to build a simple agent that uses tools and resources to improve a workflow.


The same thinking applies to managers. Instead of asking only which tasks AI can automate, consider how it could improve your team’s performance. Ask yourself: What’s the gap between what we can accomplish today and what we want to accomplish tomorrow? What skills would help my team close that gap?


## Develop and demonstrate your skills wallet


When evaluating someone’s qualifications, I’m interested not just in their job titles or background but in what they can actually do—their skills wallet.


Certificates and credentials can help showcase skills as you acquire them. Completing a course from a recognized organization demonstrates an investment in learning, while more extensive specializations may provide additional evidence of your capabilities. But credentials are even more powerful when paired with examples of how you’ve applied your skills. Being able to explain how you improved a workflow or solved a problem shows employers what you can accomplish with AI.


Ultimately, choosing the right AI course isn’t about following trends or collecting credentials. It’s about understanding where you are, deciding where you want to go and building the skills to get you there.
